3/1.about: A mournful, songlike lament in E-flat minor. A long, darkly coloured melody unfolds over slow, sombre chords, and the piece is one of the most intense of Rachmaninoff’s early miniatures.
3/1.ctx: The first of the five Morceaux de fantaisie, Op. 3, composed in 1892 when Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had just graduated from the Moscow Conservatory. The set is dedicated to his teacher Anton Arensky.
facts: The first of the five Morceaux de fantaisie.

3/2.about: Nicknamed the ’Bells of Moscow’, this brief, weighty prelude became Rachmaninoff’s most famous single piece almost overnight, built on three massive, tolling chords that open the work and return to close it, framing an agitated, stormy central section. Rachmaninoff grew to resent the piece’s overwhelming popularity, which followed him for the rest of his life and which audiences constantly demanded as an encore.
3/2.ctx: Composed in 1892 when Rachmaninoff was only nineteen, part of a set of five character pieces, Op. 3, dedicated to his teacher Anton Arensky. Its sudden fame abroad, especially in America, meant Rachmaninoff, decades later, still could rarely give a recital without being asked to play it.
facts: Rachmaninoff’s first major success, composed at just nineteen.
He grew to resent how often audiences demanded it as an encore.
Known popularly as the ’Bells of Moscow’.

3/3.about: A tender, lyrical melody in E major, sung in the tenor register with a flowing accompaniment. Its warm, songlike character shows the young composer’s gift for long-breathed melody.
3/3.ctx: Rachmaninoff revised the piece in 1940 and made a well-known recording of the revised version. It is the third of the five Morceaux de fantaisie, Op. 3.
facts: The third of the Morceaux de fantaisie.

3/4.about: A quick, capricious scherzo in F-sharp minor, full of leaping staccato figures. The piece portrays Polichinelle, the French form of the commedia dell’arte clown Punch.
3/4.ctx: The fourth of the five Morceaux de fantaisie. Polichinelle is the French name for the clown Pulcinella, and the piece has remained a favourite of pianists as an encore.
facts: Polichinelle is the French version of Punch.
The fourth of the Morceaux de fantaisie.
A showpiece of staccato and leaps.

3/5.about: A Spanish-flavoured serenade in B-flat minor with a guitar-like accompaniment beneath a wistful, expressive melody. It has a graceful, quietly passionate character.
3/5.ctx: The last of the five Morceaux de fantaisie, Op. 3, dedicated to Arensky. The set was published in 1893, when Rachmaninoff was still a student.
facts: The last of the Morceaux de fantaisie.

23/1.about: A slow, brooding prelude in F-sharp minor, marked Largo, with a long, sombre melody and rich, flowing harmony. It is among the most introspective of the set.
23/1.ctx: One of the ten preludes of Op. 23, composed between 1901 and 1903 and dedicated to Rachmaninoff’s cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti. Together with the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the Op. 32 set, they complete a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys.

23/2.about: A majestic, virtuosic prelude in B-flat major, with sweeping figures in the left hand and rich chords. It is reminiscent in places of Chopin’s ‘Revolutionary’ Étude.
23/2.ctx: One of the ten preludes of Op. 23, composed between 1901 and 1903 and dedicated to Rachmaninoff’s cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti. Together with the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the Op. 32 set, they complete a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys.

23/3.about: A stately, dance-like prelude in D minor, marked Tempo di minuetto, with a sardonic, faintly sinister character. Its crisp rhythms and spiky staccato give it a mocking edge.
23/3.ctx: One of the ten preludes of Op. 23, composed between 1901 and 1903 and dedicated to Rachmaninoff’s cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti. Together with the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the Op. 32 set, they complete a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys.

23/4.about: A lyrical prelude in D major with a long-breathed melody and flowing accompaniment, like a nocturne. The minor mood is never far away.
23/4.ctx: One of the ten preludes of Op. 23, composed between 1901 and 1903 and dedicated to Rachmaninoff’s cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti. Together with the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the Op. 32 set, they complete a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys.

23/5.about: Marked ’Alla marcia’, one of Rachmaninoff’s most popular preludes, built on a bold, martial main theme framing a broad, lyrical central melody, combining the composer’s gift for sweeping Romantic melody with a driving rhythmic energy.
23/5.ctx: Composed in 1901, part of the ten preludes of Op. 23 written in the years following the triumphant success of the Second Piano Concerto, after Rachmaninoff had emerged from the severe depression and creative block that had followed the disastrous premiere of his First Symphony.
facts: One of the most frequently performed of Rachmaninoff’s twenty-four preludes.
Composed in the productive years following the success of his Second Piano Concerto.
Marked ’Alla marcia’ for its bold, march-like character.

23/6.about: A tender, flowing prelude in E-flat major, built around a three-note melodic figure that is repeated in constant variation over a rippling accompaniment.
23/6.ctx: One of the ten preludes of Op. 23, composed between 1901 and 1903 and dedicated to Rachmaninoff’s cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti. Together with the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the Op. 32 set, they complete a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys.
facts: Built on repeated variations of a short melodic idea.

23/7.about: A restless, cascading prelude in C minor, marked Allegro, with a torrent of notes and a driving, stormy character.
23/7.ctx: One of the ten preludes of Op. 23, composed between 1901 and 1903 and dedicated to Rachmaninoff’s cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti. Together with the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the Op. 32 set, they complete a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys.

23/8.about: A sparkling, rippling prelude in A-flat major, marked Allegro vivace, with a light, flowing texture and a warm, expressive melody.
23/8.ctx: One of the ten preludes of Op. 23, composed between 1901 and 1903 and dedicated to Rachmaninoff’s cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti. Together with the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the Op. 32 set, they complete a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys.

23/9.about: A rapid, perpetual-motion prelude in E-flat minor, marked Presto, built largely on double notes and constantly shifting harmony. It is one of the most difficult of the set.
23/9.ctx: One of the ten preludes of Op. 23, composed between 1901 and 1903 and dedicated to Rachmaninoff’s cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti. Together with the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the Op. 32 set, they complete a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys.
facts: One of the most difficult of the set.

23/10.about: A quiet, contemplative prelude in G-flat major, marked Largo, that ends the set in a mood of hushed reflection with rich, full harmonies.
23/10.ctx: One of the ten preludes of Op. 23, composed between 1901 and 1903 and dedicated to Rachmaninoff’s cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti. Together with the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the Op. 32 set, they complete a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys.

32/1.about: A brief, fiery opener in C major, marked Allegro vivace, with bold, brilliant gestures.
32/1.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.
facts: The first of thirteen preludes in Op. 32.
One of the shortest of the set.

32/2.about: A gentle, lilting prelude in B-flat minor, marked Allegretto, in the manner of a barcarolle.
32/2.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/3.about: A vigorous, festive prelude in E major, marked Allegro vivace, with bold, ringing chords.
32/3.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/4.about: A dramatic, wide-ranging prelude in E minor, marked Allegro con brio, with stormy, sweeping figures.
32/4.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/5.about: A serene, shimmering prelude in G major, marked Moderato, with a flowing melody over a gently rippling accompaniment. It is one of Rachmaninoff’s most beloved short pieces.
32/5.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/6.about: A short, violent outburst in F minor, marked Allegro appassionato, with sharp, pounding rhythms and sudden bursts of passion.
32/6.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/7.about: A lyrical, gently flowing prelude in F major, marked Moderato, with a calm, songlike melody.
32/7.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/8.about: A restless, flickering prelude in A minor, marked Vivace, with light, quick figuration.
32/8.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/9.about: A dreamy prelude in A major, marked Allegro moderato, built on rippling triplet figures.
32/9.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/10.about: A brooding, desolate prelude in B minor, marked Lento, with a passionate central section. It is one of Rachmaninoff’s own favourites and is linked to Arnold Böcklin’s painting ‘The Return’.
32/10.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/11.about: A delicate, rhythmic prelude in B major, marked Allegretto, with a light, graceful character.
32/11.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.

32/12.about: A restless, melancholy prelude built on rippling, unbroken figuration under a wistful melody, often considered one of the most purely beautiful of Rachmaninoff’s twenty-four preludes, which together span every major and minor key in the tradition of Chopin’s Op. 28 and Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier.
32/12.ctx: Composed in 1910 at Ivanovka, the Rachmaninoff family estate, as the last of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, completing his cycle of twenty-four preludes across three opus numbers (Op. 3 No. 2, Op. 23, and Op. 32) that together cover all twenty-four keys.
facts: Completes Rachmaninoff’s cycle of twenty-four preludes across three opus numbers.
Composed at Ivanovka, the Rachmaninoff family’s country estate.
Regarded as one of the most lyrically beautiful of his preludes.

32/13.about: A grand, triumphant finale in D-flat major, marked Grave, that closes the complete cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys with broad, ringing chords.
32/13.ctx: One of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, composed in the summer of 1910 at Rachmaninoff’s family estate of Ivanovka. With the Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2, and the ten preludes of Op. 23, the set completes a cycle of preludes in all twenty-four keys. Op. 32 carries no dedication.
facts: Closes the cycle of twenty-four preludes.
The last of thirteen preludes in Op. 32.

33.about: A set of eight études-tableaux, or ‘study-pictures’, that combine virtuoso technical demands with vivid, evocative character. Rachmaninoff refused to say what images inspired them, believing listeners should paint their own.
33.ctx: Composed in August–September 1911 at Ivanovka, the year after the Op. 32 preludes. Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux (‘study-pictures’) but published only six in 1914. The remaining études were published after his death. He once said he did not believe in the artist who discloses too much of his images.
parts: A sombre study, unpublished in his lifetime.
A study of sharp contrasts and brilliant figuration.
facts: Rachmaninoff refused to reveal what inspired them.
He wrote nine but published only six.
Ottorino Respighi orchestrated some of them in 1930.

33/1.about: A brusque, march-like study in F minor, marked Allegro non troppo, with heavy chords and driving rhythm.
33/1.ctx: Composed in August–September 1911 at Ivanovka, the year after the Op. 32 preludes. Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux (‘study-pictures’) but published only six in 1914.
facts: The first of the Op. 33 études-tableaux.

33/2.about: A flowing, lyrical study in C major, marked Allegro, in which a long melody floats over a rippling accompaniment.
33/2.ctx: Composed in August–September 1911 at Ivanovka, the year after the Op. 32 preludes. Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux (‘study-pictures’) but published only six in 1914.

33/3.about: A sombre, slow study in C minor, marked Grave, with heavy, solemn textures.
33/3.ctx: Composed in August–September 1911 at Ivanovka, the year after the Op. 32 preludes. Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux (‘study-pictures’) but published only six in 1914. Rachmaninoff withheld it from publication, and its material is said to have been reused in the slow movement of his Fourth Piano Concerto.
facts: Its material was later reused in the Fourth Piano Concerto.

33/4.about: A dark, march-tinged study in D minor, marked Moderato, with a brooding, heavy character.
33/4.ctx: Composed in August–September 1911 at Ivanovka, the year after the Op. 32 preludes. Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux (‘study-pictures’) but published only six in 1914. It was withheld from the first edition.

33/5.about: A rapid, whispering study in E-flat minor, marked Non allegro – Presto, in which quick, light figures rush past like shadows.
33/5.ctx: Composed in August–September 1911 at Ivanovka, the year after the Op. 32 preludes. Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux (‘study-pictures’) but published only six in 1914.

33/6.about: A festive, brilliant study in E-flat major, marked Allegro con fuoco, with ringing chords and sparkling energy.
33/6.ctx: Composed in August–September 1911 at Ivanovka, the year after the Op. 32 preludes. Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux (‘study-pictures’) but published only six in 1914.

33/7.about: A study of sharp contrasts in G minor, marked Moderato, with brilliant figuration and sudden changes of mood.
33/7.ctx: Composed in August–September 1911 at Ivanovka, the year after the Op. 32 preludes. Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux (‘study-pictures’) but published only six in 1914.

33/8.about: A dramatic study in C-sharp minor, marked Grave, with a tolling, bell-like bass and imposing chords. It closes the Op. 33 set with weight.
33/8.ctx: Composed in August–September 1911 at Ivanovka, the year after the Op. 32 preludes. Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux (‘study-pictures’) but published only six in 1914.

39.about: Nine large-scale study-pictures, denser, darker and more ambitious than the Op. 33 set. Rachmaninoff again declined to describe what inspired them, though he later shared a few images with Ottorino Respighi, who orchestrated several of them.
39.ctx: Composed in 1916–17 in Moscow and at Ivanovka, the Op. 39 études-tableaux were the last works Rachmaninoff wrote before leaving Russia in December 1917. He reportedly told Respighi that Nos. 2 and 6 depicted a seascape with seagulls and the story of Little Red Riding Hood, No. 7 a funeral procession and No. 9 an oriental march.
parts: A haunting seascape known as ‘The Sea and Seagulls’.
Little Red Riding Hood and the wolf.
facts: Rachmaninoff’s last piano works written in Russia.
Respighi orchestrated several of them in 1930.
No. 6 is a revision of a lost étude from Op. 33.

39/1.about: A stormy, turbulent study in C minor, marked Allegro agitato, with urgent, driving rhythms and heavy chords.
39/1.ctx: Composed in 1916–17 in Moscow and at Ivanovka, the Op. 39 études-tableaux were the last works Rachmaninoff wrote before leaving Russia in December 1917. It is the first of the nine.

39/2.about: A haunting, rocking seascape in A minor, marked Lento assai, in which slow, heaving figures suggest waves and the cries of seagulls. It is often known as ‘The Sea and Seagulls’.
39/2.ctx: Composed in 1916–17 in Moscow and at Ivanovka, the Op. 39 études-tableaux were the last works Rachmaninoff wrote before leaving Russia in December 1917. Rachmaninoff reportedly described this image to Respighi.
facts: Rachmaninoff shared the image with Respighi.

39/3.about: A driving, restless study in F-sharp minor, marked Allegro molto, with rapid figuration and urgent energy.
39/3.ctx: Composed in 1916–17 in Moscow and at Ivanovka, the Op. 39 études-tableaux were the last works Rachmaninoff wrote before leaving Russia in December 1917. It is the third of the nine.

39/4.about: A lively, humorous study in B minor, marked Allegro assai, with quick, playful figures.
39/4.ctx: Composed in 1916–17 in Moscow and at Ivanovka, the Op. 39 études-tableaux were the last works Rachmaninoff wrote before leaving Russia in December 1917. It is the fourth of the nine.

39/5.about: One of the most passionate and frequently performed of Rachmaninoff’s Étude-tableaux, marked ’Appassionato’, built on a driving, obsessive rhythmic figure and sweeping melodic lines of enormous emotional intensity.
39/5.ctx: Composed in 1916–17, among the last works Rachmaninoff completed in Russia before fleeing the country permanently following the 1917 Revolution, part of the second set of Étude-tableaux, Op. 39, whose titled ’picture studies’ Rachmaninoff deliberately left mysterious, refusing in most cases to explain what images inspired them.
facts: Composed shortly before Rachmaninoff permanently left Russia after the 1917 Revolution.
Marked ’Appassionato’ for its intense, driving character.
Rachmaninoff generally declined to explain the specific images behind his Étude-tableaux.

39/6.about: A quick, menacing study in A minor, marked Allegro, with growling wolf-like sonorities and scurrying figures. It is often called ‘Little Red Riding Hood’.
39/6.ctx: Composed in 1916–17 in Moscow and at Ivanovka, the Op. 39 études-tableaux were the last works Rachmaninoff wrote before leaving Russia in December 1917. It is a revision of an earlier étude from the Op. 33 group that was lost. Rachmaninoff reportedly described the picture as Little Red Riding Hood and the wolf.
facts: A revision of a lost earlier étude.

39/7.about: A grave, slow study in C minor, marked Lento lugubre, with a heavy, funeral-march-like rhythm and tolling bells.
39/7.ctx: Composed in 1916–17 in Moscow and at Ivanovka, the Op. 39 études-tableaux were the last works Rachmaninoff wrote before leaving Russia in December 1917. Rachmaninoff reportedly said it depicted a funeral procession.

39/8.about: A lyrical, flowing study in D minor, marked Allegro moderato, in which a warm melody is set against a rippling accompaniment.
39/8.ctx: Composed in 1916–17 in Moscow and at Ivanovka, the Op. 39 études-tableaux were the last works Rachmaninoff wrote before leaving Russia in December 1917. It is the eighth of the nine.

39/9.about: A festive, march-like finale in D major, marked Tempo di marcia, with ringing chords and driving rhythms.
39/9.ctx: Composed in 1916–17 in Moscow and at Ivanovka, the Op. 39 études-tableaux were the last works Rachmaninoff wrote before leaving Russia in December 1917. Rachmaninoff reportedly described it as an oriental march.

16/1.about: A long, songlike melody in B-flat minor over a rippling accompaniment, in the style of a nocturne. The mood is plaintive and the tune keeps returning with new ornament.
16/1.ctx: Composed in the autumn of 1896 and published in 1897, the six Moments musicaux, Op. 16, are dedicated to Alexander Zatayevich. The title recalls Schubert’s set of the same name. They were written shortly before the disastrous premiere of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony in 1897.
facts: The first of six Moments musicaux.

16/2.about: A swirling, turbulent study in E-flat minor, in which restless figures in the right hand rush over a driving bass. It is quick and brilliant.
16/2.ctx: Composed in the autumn of 1896 and published in 1897, the six Moments musicaux, Op. 16, are dedicated to Alexander Zatayevich. The title recalls Schubert’s set of the same name. They were written shortly before the disastrous premiere of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony in 1897.
facts: The second of six Moments musicaux.

16/3.about: A sombre, funereal piece in B minor, with a solemn chordal theme and a dark, lamenting character. It builds to an impressive climax before fading.
16/3.ctx: Composed in the autumn of 1896 and published in 1897, the six Moments musicaux, Op. 16, are dedicated to Alexander Zatayevich. The title recalls Schubert’s set of the same name. They were written shortly before the disastrous premiere of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony in 1897.
facts: The third of six Moments musicaux.
Has the character of a funeral march.

16/4.about: A stormy, virtuosic study in E minor, marked Presto, of rapid figures and fierce energy. It is one of the most demanding pieces in the set.
16/4.ctx: Composed in the autumn of 1896 and published in 1897, the six Moments musicaux, Op. 16, are dedicated to Alexander Zatayevich. The title recalls Schubert’s set of the same name. They were written shortly before the disastrous premiere of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony in 1897.
facts: The fourth of six Moments musicaux.
One of the most technically demanding of the set.

16/5.about: A calm, rocking barcarolle in D-flat major, with a lyrical melody floating over a gentle, flowing accompaniment. It is among the most serene of Rachmaninoff’s early works.
16/5.ctx: Composed in the autumn of 1896 and published in 1897, the six Moments musicaux, Op. 16, are dedicated to Alexander Zatayevich. The title recalls Schubert’s set of the same name. They were written shortly before the disastrous premiere of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony in 1897.
facts: The fifth of six Moments musicaux.
Written in the style of a barcarolle.

16/6.about: A grand, triumphant finale in C major, with a stately theme and ringing, full-toned piano writing. It closes the set with a blaze of virtuosity.
16/6.ctx: Composed in the autumn of 1896 and published in 1897, the six Moments musicaux, Op. 16, are dedicated to Alexander Zatayevich. The title recalls Schubert’s set of the same name. They were written shortly before the disastrous premiere of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony in 1897.
facts: The last of six Moments musicaux.
Ends the set in C major.

1.about: A youthful, brilliant concerto in F-sharp minor, full of energy, lyricism and virtuosity. Its themes are memorable, and the finale sparkles with vivacity. In 1917 Rachmaninoff thoroughly revised it, and the revised version is the one usually played.
1.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed it at seventeen and eighteen, modelling its outer movements on Grieg’s concerto, which he admired. He played the first movement at a student concert in March 1892, with Vasily Safonov conducting. He dedicated it to his cousin and teacher Alexander Siloti. In 1917, shortly before leaving Russia, he revised it thoroughly.
parts: A bold opening leading into a lyrical main theme.

18.about: Rachmaninoff’s most beloved and frequently performed concerto, marking his triumphant return to composition after a severe depression and creative paralysis following the disastrous 1897 premiere of his First Symphony. Its sweeping opening chords, soaring melodies and hard-won emotional journey from darkness to triumph have made it one of the most popular concertos ever written.
18.ctx: Composed in 1900–01 after months of therapy with the physician Nikolai Dahl, whose hypnosis-based treatment Rachmaninoff credited with restoring his ability to compose; the concerto is dedicated to Dahl in gratitude. Its success re-established Rachmaninoff’s career and remains, over a century later, one of the most recorded and performed works in the entire concerto repertoire.
parts: Famous for its tolling opening piano chords leading into a passionate main theme.
A serene, deeply lyrical slow movement.
A vigorous finale that transforms its themes into a triumphant close.
facts: Dedicated to Dr. Nikolai Dahl, whose treatment helped Rachmaninoff overcome a severe creative block.
Marked his return to composing after the failed premiere of his First Symphony.
One of the most popular and frequently performed piano concertos ever written.

30.about: Nicknamed ’Rach 3’ by pianists, one of the most technically formidable concertos in the repertoire, composed for Rachmaninoff’s first American tour and dedicated to the pianist Josef Hofmann, who reportedly never performed it in public, considering it not suited to his own hands. Its immense difficulty and emotional scope made it, decades later, the subject of the 1996 film Shine.
30.ctx: Composed in 1909 at Ivanovka in preparation for Rachmaninoff’s debut tour of the United States, where he premiered it himself in New York that November under the young conductor Walter Damrosch, and again weeks later under Gustav Mahler, of whose rehearsal discipline Rachmaninoff spoke admiringly.
parts: A famous, deceptively simple opening theme leading to enormous technical and emotional demands.
facts: Popularly nicknamed ’Rach 3’ for its extraordinary technical demands.
Its dedicatee, Josef Hofmann, reportedly never performed it publicly.
The subject of the 1996 film Shine, about pianist David Helfgott.

40.about: A restless, lean concerto in G minor, lighter in texture than the Second and Third, with sharper themes and a wry, sometimes jazz-tinged modernity. Its slow movement is a sombre Largo, and the finale is fast and rhythmic.
40.ctx: Rachmaninoff worked on the concerto in 1926, drawing on ideas that go back to 1911. The premiere in Philadelphia in March 1927, with Leopold Stokowski conducting, was coldly received. He revised it in 1927 and again in 1941, and the last version is the one usually played. It is dedicated to his friend Nikolai Medtner.
facts: Premiered in Philadelphia with Stokowski conducting.

43.about: A set of twenty-four variations on the famous theme of Paganini’s 24th Caprice for solo violin, alternating brilliant virtuoso display with passages of deep lyricism, most famously the eighteenth variation, which inverts Paganini’s theme into a soaring, romantic melody that became one of Rachmaninoff’s most beloved tunes, later used in countless films.
43.ctx: Composed in 1934 at Rachmaninoff’s villa in Switzerland, one of the last major works he completed, drawing on the same Paganini theme that had already inspired variation sets by Brahms and Liszt, and incorporating, in several stormy variations, a quotation of the medieval Dies irae chant that recurs throughout much of Rachmaninoff’s output.
facts: Its famous 18th variation inverts Paganini’s theme into a soaring new melody.
One of the last major works Rachmaninoff completed.
Quotes the medieval Dies irae chant, a recurring motif throughout his music.

28.about: A massive, dark sonata in D minor, with three large movements that are rich in themes and demanding in technique. It was originally conceived with Goethe’s Faust in mind, and its movements were to portray Faust, Gretchen and Mephistopheles.
28.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed it in Dresden while also writing his Second Symphony, then cut it substantially on the advice of friends. Konstantin Igumnov gave the first performance in Moscow in October 1908. It is one of his least performed works.

36.about: A large-scale, densely virtuosic sonata that Rachmaninoff substantially revised nearly two decades after its composition, cutting and simplifying its most sprawling passages; both versions remain in the repertoire, with pianists divided over which better represents the composer’s intentions.
36.ctx: Composed in 1913 while Rachmaninoff was staying in Rome, in rooms once used by Tchaikovsky’s brother, and extensively revised in 1931 into a shorter, leaner version, reflecting Rachmaninoff’s own later view that the original had been overwritten.
parts: A turbulent, densely written opening movement.
facts: Rachmaninoff extensively revised the sonata in 1931, nearly two decades after its premiere.
Both the 1913 and 1931 versions remain in active use by performers today.
Composed in rooms in Rome once used by Tchaikovsky’s brother.

13.about: A dark, ambitious symphony in D minor, rich in thematic ideas and full of Russian character. Its four movements are linked by a motto theme based on chant, and the finale ends in a blaze of D major.
13.ctx: Rachmaninoff finished it in 1895. The premiere in St Petersburg in 1897 under Alexander Glazunov was a disaster, and the reviews were savage: César Cui wrote that if there were a conservatory in hell, the symphony would win its prize. Rachmaninoff fell into depression and did not compose seriously for three years. The score was lost, and the work was reconstructed from parts found in 1944.
parts: A slow introduction leading into a stormy Allegro.
facts: The disastrous premiere caused a creative crisis.
The score was lost and later reconstructed from orchestral parts.

27.about: A large-scale, richly melodic symphony, in particular its third movement, an extended Adagio built on one of Rachmaninoff’s most celebrated melodies, which has been adapted into popular songs and used widely in film. Composed as an act of redemption after the traumatic failure of his First Symphony a decade earlier.
27.ctx: Composed in 1906–07 while Rachmaninoff was living in Dresden, partly to escape the demands of his busy Moscow performing career and concentrate on composition, the symphony was a triumphant success at its premiere, helping to heal the deep insecurity left by his earlier symphonic failure.
parts: A brooding introduction leading to a sweeping main movement.
The symphony’s famous, richly melodic slow movement.
facts: Its slow movement contains one of Rachmaninoff’s most famous melodies.
Composed in Dresden, partly to escape his demanding Moscow concert schedule.
A triumphant success that helped heal the wounds of his earlier symphonic failure.

44.about: A nostalgic, rhythmically vital symphony in A minor, with a motto theme that returns throughout the work. The orchestration is subtle and finely coloured, and the mood shifts between wistfulness and energy.
44.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed it at the Villa Senar, his lakeside home in Switzerland, between 1935 and 1936. The premiere in Philadelphia in November 1936 received a mixed reception, and he revised it in 1938. It is his last symphony.
parts: A motto theme opens the work.
Adagio ma non troppo – Allegro vivace
A slow movement with a quick scherzo at its heart.

45.about: Rachmaninoff’s last completed work, a three-movement orchestral suite of enormous colour and nostalgia, incorporating a quotation of his own long-abandoned First Symphony in the first movement and, in the finale, the Dies irae chant set finally against a quotation of the Orthodox ’Blessed art Thou, O Lord’ from his All-Night Vigil — read by many as the composer’s own farewell.
45.ctx: Composed in 1940 at Rachmaninoff’s summer home on Long Island, the last major work he completed before his death three years later, drawing together threads — the Dies irae, Orthodox chant, echoes of his own earlier music — that had run through his entire creative life.
parts: A nostalgic opening movement quoting Rachmaninoff’s own First Symphony.
A finale combining the Dies irae with a quotation from his own All-Night Vigil.
facts: Quotes his own First Symphony and his choral work All-Night Vigil.
Widely interpreted as the composer’s musical farewell.

29.about: A somber orchestral tone poem inspired by Arnold Böcklin’s famous painting of the same name, depicting a shrouded figure being rowed toward a mysterious island of cypress trees and tombs. Built in an unusual, irregular 5/8 metre suggesting the slow, uneven strokes of oars, the piece grows increasingly turbulent before subsiding into a hushed, resigned close.
29.ctx: Composed in 1908–09 in Dresden, inspired specifically by a black-and-white photographic reproduction of Böcklin’s painting rather than the original, which Rachmaninoff reportedly found less striking in colour; quotes the Dies irae chant recurrent throughout his output.
facts: Inspired by Arnold Böcklin’s painting of the same name.
Rachmaninoff based it on a black-and-white photograph of the painting rather than the coloured original.
Written in an unusual 5/8 metre suggesting the rhythm of oars.

34/14.about: A wordless song for voice and piano, sung entirely on a vowel sound without text, built on one long, arching melodic line of extraordinary simplicity and emotional directness; it has become one of Rachmaninoff’s most beloved melodies, frequently arranged for cello, violin, orchestra and countless other combinations.
34/14.ctx: Composed in 1912 as the last of the Fourteen Songs, Op. 34, dedicated to the soprano Antonina Nezhdanova, who premiered it; the absence of any text has made the piece endlessly adaptable to instrumental arrangement, and it is now probably better known in its many instrumental versions than in its original vocal form.
34/14.sc: Voice and piano (or various instrumental arrangements)
facts: Sung entirely on a vowel sound, with no text.
Dedicated to the soprano Antonina Nezhdanova, who premiered it.
Now most often heard in one of its many instrumental arrangements.

42.about: A set of twenty variations on a theme by Corelli (in fact borrowed, unknowingly by Corelli himself, from an older Portuguese folk tune known as ’La Folia’), alternating brilliant virtuosity with passages of stark, austere beauty; among the last solo piano works Rachmaninoff completed.
42.ctx: Composed in 1931 in Switzerland, where Rachmaninoff had settled after leaving Russia, the piece reflects the leaner, more concentrated style of his later works, a contrast to the lush Romantic sweep of his earlier Russian-period music.
facts: Based on the ’La Folia’ theme long misattributed to Corelli.
Among the last solo piano works Rachmaninoff completed.
Written in his leaner, more concentrated later style.

22.about: A set of twenty-two variations on the Prelude in C minor from Chopin’s Op. 28, which appears as a stately, chordal theme. The variations move from delicate ornament to stormy virtuosity, and the work is Rachmaninoff’s first large-scale piece for solo piano.
22.ctx: Composed in 1902–03 and dedicated to the pianist and teacher Theodor Leschetizky. It was written at the same time as the Op. 23 preludes and first performed in Moscow in February 1903.
facts: Based on Chopin’s Prelude in C minor, Op. 28 No. 20.
Rachmaninoff’s first large-scale solo piano work.

19.about: A lyrical sonata in G minor in which the piano is treated as an equal partner, with a richly written and demanding part. Its four movements range from a solemn introduction to a warm, songlike slow movement and a sweeping finale.
19.ctx: Rachmaninoff finished it in November 1901 shortly after the triumph of the Second Piano Concerto and gave the premiere with the cellist Anatoly Brandukov, its dedicatee, in Moscow in December. He made a few changes after the premiere.
parts: A slow introduction leads into the first theme.
facts: Dedicated to the cellist Anatoly Brandukov.
The piano part is unusually rich.
Completed shortly after the Second Piano Concerto.

9.ded: To the memory of a great artist (Tchaikovsky)
9.about: A grief-stricken piano trio in D minor, written in memory of Tchaikovsky. The piano part is florid and important, and the music has a passionate, elegiac quality that builds to intense climaxes.
9.ctx: Rachmaninoff began it on hearing of Tchaikovsky’s death in October 1893 and finished it in December. He dedicated it ‘to the memory of a great artist’. It was first performed in Moscow in January 1894 with Rachmaninoff at the piano, and he revised it in 1907 and 1917.
parts: A lament that builds to a passionate climax.
A set of variations on a plaintive theme.
A short, intense finale that recalls the lament.
facts: Dedicated ‘to the memory of a great artist’.

5.about: A suite of four poetic pictures for two pianos, each prefaced by a poem: a barcarolle, a night of love, tears and Easter. The two piano parts interweave and evoke the sounds of bells, especially in the finale.
5.ctx: Composed in 1893, when Rachmaninoff was twenty, and dedicated to Tchaikovsky. The four epigraphs are by Lermontov, Byron, Tyutchev and Khomyakov. The bell sounds of the finale foreshadow The Bells.
parts: A warm nocturne of night and love.
A brilliant Easter finale with pealing bells.
facts: Each movement has a poetic epigraph.

17.about: A brilliant suite for two pianos in four movements: a stately march-like Introduction, a glittering Valse, a tender Romance and a whirling Tarantelle. The two pianists are equal partners, and the music has the sweep and warmth of the Second Piano Concerto.
17.ctx: Composed at the same time as the Second Piano Concerto, in the months after Rachmaninoff’s recovery from his creative crisis, and dedicated to his future wife Natalia Satina. The suite is one of the most popular works for two pianos.
facts: Composed at the same time as the Second Piano Concerto.
The Tarantelle is a famous virtuoso finale.

37.ded: To the memory of Stepan Smolensky
37.about: A setting for unaccompanied mixed choir of the Russian Orthodox all-night vigil service, in fifteen movements. Rachmaninoff draws on ancient chant and writes freely in its style, with rich choral textures and a famously low bass part.
37.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed it in a couple of weeks in early 1915, during the First World War, and dedicated it to the memory of Stepan Smolensky, an authority on Russian church music. The first performance was given by the Moscow Synodal Choir in March 1915. He asked that one of its movements be sung at his funeral.
facts: Dedicated to the memory of Stepan Smolensky.
Contains a famously low part for basses.

35.ded: Willem Mengelberg and the Concertgebouw Orchestra
35.about: A choral symphony in four movements for soprano, tenor and baritone soloists, chorus and orchestra, on Poe’s poem ‘The Bells’ in Konstantin Balmont’s Russian version. The four kinds of bell (sleigh, wedding, alarm and funeral) give the work its structure and its drama.
35.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed it in 1913, mainly in Rome, and dedicated it to the conductor Willem Mengelberg and the Concertgebouw Orchestra. He is said to have considered it his favourite among his own works.
parts: Sleigh bells of youth and joy.
Golden bells of love and marriage.
Brazen bells of terror and fire.
Iron bells of death and silence.
35.sc: Soprano, tenor and baritone soloists, chorus and orchestra
facts: Based on Poe’s poem ‘The Bells’ in Balmont’s Russian version.
Dedicated to Willem Mengelberg and the Concertgebouw Orchestra.
Reputedly Rachmaninoff’s favourite of his own works.

21/5.about: A delicate song about the scent of lilacs, in which the fragrance of the flowers becomes a symbol of happiness. The vocal line is gentle and the piano accompaniment shimmers quietly.
21/5.ctx: ‘Lilacs’ is the fifth of twelve songs in Op. 21, to a poem by Ekaterina Beketova. Rachmaninoff himself made a piano transcription, which has become a popular recital piece.
facts: Rachmaninoff made a piano transcription himself.
Sets a poem by Ekaterina Beketova.
One of twelve songs in Op. 21.

38/3.about: A charming, quick song about daisies, in which the piano writing sparkles and the vocal line has a light, dancing grace. It is one of the most popular of Rachmaninoff’s later songs.
38/3.ctx: ‘Daisies’ is the third of six songs in Op. 38, setting poems by Russian symbolist poets, in this case Igor Severyanin. Rachmaninoff also made a piano transcription of it.
facts: Sets a poem by Igor Severyanin.
One of six songs in Op. 38.

10/5.about: A playful, scherzo-like piece in G major, full of light, dance-like staccato and delicate humour. It is one of the most cheerful of the early Morceaux de salon.
10/5.ctx: The fifth of the seven Morceaux de salon, Op. 10, composed in 1894 when Rachmaninoff was in his early twenties. The set includes a nocturne, a waltz, a barcarolle, a melody, a humoresque, a romance and a mazurka.
facts: The fifth of seven Morceaux de salon.
Marked with a playful, scherzo character.
